routes.description: Establish that an unlimited, value-supreme, personal necessary foundation unifies ultimate reality and explains irreducible mind with fewer independent primitives.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if supremacy yields the relevant attributes without added fundamental complexity and better unifies necessary reality, value, and consciousness.

motionBridge.description: Show that a supreme personal foundation better accounts for ultimate reality, mind, and worldview simplicity than a nonmental initial reality.

centralBridges.description: Show that removing arbitrary foundational limits supports supreme value and its substantive implications.
Show that one supreme foundation explains multiple necessary domains with fewer independent primitives.
Show that consciousness has irreducible features predicted and producible by a supreme mental foundation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Justify using philosophical evidence from logic, value, mathematics, and consciousness alongside physical evidence.
Preserve focused comparisons of theoretical virtues while situating them within the complete worldview comparison.

routes.description: Establish that a necessary nonmental initial reality, continuous with later nature, avoids unwarranted primordial mentality and explains minds through neural functioning.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if foundational mentality and supremacy remain additional commitments while naturalistic continuity, neural identity, and total-package comparison remain adequate.

motionBridge.description: Show that a naturalistic initial reality better accounts for ultimate reality, evolved mind, and total worldview simplicity than a supreme personal foundation.

centralBridges.description: Characterize the necessary initial reality as causally continuous with later nature without primordial mentality.
Show that mentality and divine attributes add substantive structure not obtained merely by removing limits.
Show that appropriately situated neural functioning can fully account for conscious states.
Require simplicity and explanatory fit to be assessed across the complete disputed commitments of each worldview.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require adequate evidence before assigning rich properties to the unknown initial reality.
Allow logic, morality, value, and physical origins to have independent foundations rather than one common source.

sectionSelections.title: Category and continuity of initial reality
sectionSelections.rationale: The characterization of the necessary initial reality determines whether the comparison requires an additional ontological category or permits continuity with later concrete reality.

proSelections.proposition: A necessary foundational reality may count as natural when it is intelligible, scientifically investigable, and in the same basic category as other concrete things.

conSelections.proposition: Once shared causal history and ordinary composition are held fixed, the principal worldview disagreement concerns the character of the necessary initial reality.
A naturalistic initial reality is necessary yet causally continuous with later reality, whereas some theologies introduce sharper discontinuities between God and creation.

sectionSelections.title: Unlimited supremacy and foundational complexity
sectionSelections.rationale: The central simplicity dispute turns on whether an unlimited supreme nature reduces arbitrary specification or instead introduces mentality and unsupported divine consequences.

proSelections.proposition: Among limited, unlimited, and noncommittal descriptions of the necessary initial item, specified arbitrary limits add commitments while agnosticism initially minimizes them.
Removing limits on foundational value yields a simple supreme nature whose further supreme-making attributes can be consequences rather than additional fundamental descriptions.

conSelections.proposition: Attributing consciousness or mentality to the initial reality adds substantive qualitative structure rather than merely removing arbitrary limitations.
A simple appeal to supremacy or maximal greatness does not by itself establish the required divine attributes, so deriving them requires further argument.

sectionSelections.title: Evidence, necessity, and explanatory unification
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue determines whether cross-domain evidence warrants a unified supreme source or whether necessary physical and nonphysical domains may terminate separately.

proSelections.proposition: Evidence from logic, value, mathematics, and consciousness can support a supreme foundation before fundamental physics is complete.
Explanatory unification remains valuable among necessities because a simpler foundation can entail many necessary truths with fewer independent pieces.

conSelections.proposition: Science may be the available route to the initial reality's properties, and necessity can terminate explanation without a further account.
The causally initial physical reality need not also ground logic, morality, consciousness, or value, whose foundations may be independent.

sectionSelections.title: Nature and source of consciousness
sectionSelections.rationale: The motion's mind component depends on whether consciousness is irreducible evidence for a mental foundation or identical with evolved neural functioning.

proSelections.proposition: Introspection and direct awareness disclose irreducible conscious properties that a supreme mental foundation predicts and has resources to produce.
Direct certainty about thoughts differs from inferential belief about brains and supports one substance bearing genuinely distinct mental and physical attributes.

conSelections.proposition: On the stipulated naturalism, minds are late, local products of biological evolution rather than features of the initial reality.
Consciousness is identical with appropriately situated neural functioning, and introspection cannot establish that conscious states are not neural processing.

sectionSelections.title: Scope of the worldview comparison
sectionSelections.rationale: The comparative burden requires a method for relating focused simplicity and explanatory questions to the broader balance of disputed worldview commitments.

proSelections.proposition: Examining one theoretical virtue at a time can clarify genuine differences provided a local advantage is not treated as victory in the total worldview comparison.

conSelections.proposition: Local advantages under an all-else-equal assumption do not decide between worldviews; comparison must assess their total explanatory packages.
Shared commitments permit some narrowing, but the remaining disputed worldview commitments are too extensive for a few isolated comparisons to represent the whole assessment.
